newsitem.title: UK: Global funds shy of US, wait on Japan revival.
newsitem.headline: Global funds shy of US, wait on Japan revival.

text.p: Global fund managers see a much rougher ride ahead for the US market in 1997 and are building cash and core European holdings while waiting for a convincing rebound in the Japanese markets.

"Our investment strategy in 1997 is based on the premise that the US stock market's strong period of relative outperformance is coming to an end," said ING Barings' global strategist John Reynolds. "We feel compelled to run an underweight stance."

The Dow Jones Industrial average has risen 75 percent since November 1994 but it could pierce the 7,000 barrier at some stage although the scope for further stock price appreciation will be limited by the earnings outlook.
Lehman Brothers global strategist Joe Rooney has already moved to underweight the US equity market, despite solid underlying fundamentals, because of better value and bond support elsewhere.

Funds generally expect moderate growth and low inflation in most global markets to persist, but Capel Cure Myers analyst Michael Lenhoff warns of increased volatility in 1997 "not just for smaller less liquid markets and/or for emerging markets but in larger mainstream markets such as the US and UK."

Capel Cure Myers sees a 50 basis point rise in US interest rates by the end of 1997 and is underweight both the US and Japan for sterling-based portfolios. They are neutral on UK and overseas equities, with Continental Europe and the Pacific Basin left at overweight.

CCM, ING Barings and HSBC Markets have all increased cash holdings. "We have a bias towards US bonds over equities," said ING Barings' Reynolds. "(And) a fully weighted cash position would at the very least appear advisable."
The mild threat of rate rises is not enough to douse the general world uptrend in bond markets which HSBC Markets thinks will resume in 1997 after a correction in the first quarter.
"Of the major markets, we expect only Japan and the UK to see any increase in official rates," said economist Mark Cliffe.
Another source of support for world bonds was the apparent determination of policymakers, especially in Europe, to reduce budget deficits, even in the face of disappointing growth.

Germany is widely seen holding the lid on interest rates in a bid to stave off a strengthening mark as investors escape the high yielding bond markets seen vulnerable if European Monetary Union goes ahead, and opt for the core Europe and the mark bloc.
ING Barings said the usual move for investors going defensive on the US stock market was a switch to Japan.
"However, in our view it is not yet appropriate to expect any sustained period of improved performance from the Japanese equity market," said strategist Matthew Merritt.

He sees an improved yen as "the signal of belief in self-sustaining economic expansion which would trigger us to adopt a more positive stance." Lehman Brothers' Rooney agrees. "An appreciating yen (and we expect the yen to appreciate by 13 percent against the dollar) is the only reason for an investor to want an exposure to Japanese equities."

Analyst Shaun Roache added : "We expect the dollar's cyclical period of strength to fade by Q2, not only against the yen but also against the European currency bloc...this should provide us with a timely signal for our European asset allocation."
